points: Aesthetic factors: the elements of design (colour, pattern, shape, texture and line) and principles such as proportion and balance create an attractive home that does not date quickly.
Aspect: a south-facing living room gains the most daylight and solar heat, so rooms are placed according to their use and the sun's path.
Passive solar design uses the layout, orientation and glazing of the house to capture and retain heat without mechanical systems.
Environmental factors include the use of durable, sustainable and locally sourced materials and the minimising of energy used in making them.
The house should fit its surroundings, with its scale and materials suiting the landscape and neighbouring buildings.
Site slope and drainage affect the layout of the house, the foundations and the position of the garden.
The number and ages of family members determine the number of bedrooms, the bathrooms and the amount of living space.
Storage for clothing, sports and garden equipment must be provided in proportion to the size of the family.
Teenagers need study space, and a home office may be needed where family members work from home.
Future needs are planned for by allowing space to extend, convert the attic or add a ground-floor bedroom.
Accessibility for people with disabilities requires wide doors, level access and an accessible bathroom.
Room use should be planned so that each room suits its function, such as a utility room for washing and drying.

notes.h: Energy efficiency and the BER certificate
points: Insulation in the roof, walls or cavity reduces heat loss, and double glazing reduces heat loss through windows.
Heating systems can be made efficient with zoned heating, thermostats and timers, or geothermal heating.
A BER certificate rates energy efficiency on a scale from A, the most efficient, to G, the least efficient.
A registered assessor measures the area of the rooms and windows, the thickness of the walls, the levels of insulation, the heating system and the floor and wall types.
A BER certificate is required when a home is sold or rented, and the rating must be shown in commercial advertisements.
Insulation, efficient heating and passive solar design all improve the BER rating and reduce running costs.
Ergonomics is the design of a space so that it suits how people move and work; in a kitchen, the sink, cooker and fridge are placed at the three points of an imaginary triangle.
Circulation space must allow people to move safely between work surfaces and to open doors and drawers without obstruction.
Switches and sockets are placed at heights that can be reached comfortably, including by children and people with limited mobility.
Sensor lights, compact fluorescent and LED lamps reduce energy use in the home.
Solar panels, thermostatic and timer controls, underfloor heating and centralised vacuum systems are technological developments that save energy or labour.
Phone-linked alarm systems and electronic gates and garage doors add security to the home.
Initial costs include the site, the builder, professional fees, materials, mortgage and legal fees and stamp duty.
Maintenance costs include cleaning, decorating, roof and gutter repair, and servicing of the heating system.
Durable, low-maintenance materials such as brick and uPVC windows reduce long-term repair and decoration costs.
Energy-efficient design lowers running costs over the life of the house, even where it adds to the initial cost.
A cheap build can cost more over time if it has poor insulation, weak materials or a costly heating system.

notes.h: Regulation of house-building standards (Higher Level only)
points: The Building Regulations set standards for the safety, materials and construction of buildings, and for insulation, heating, lighting, ventilation and waste.
Local authorities enforce the Building Regulations through building control.
Under the Building Control (Amendment) Regulations 2014, a certificate of compliance must be provided to show that completed work complies with the Building Regulations.
The National House Building Guarantee Scheme, operated by HomeBond, requires registered builders' homes to be inspected during construction and certified to standard.
A structural defects warranty such as HomeBond's covers major structural defects in a new home for a set period after completion.
HomeBond's scheme protects the deposits of buyers if a registered builder fails before completing the home.
SEAI home energy grants support insulation, heating upgrades and renewable energy such as solar panels in existing homes.

keyTerms.definition: The design of a space and its fittings to suit how people move, reach and work in it.
The direction a house or room faces, which determines how much daylight and solar heat it receives.
Designing a house's layout, orientation and glazing so that it captures and retains solar heat without mechanical systems.
A Building Energy Rating certificate that rates a home's energy efficiency from A to G.
A certificate confirming that completed building work meets the Building Regulations.
The system through which local authorities enforce the Building Regulations on new building work.
A fault in the structure of a building, such as in its foundations, walls or roof, that affects its stability.
A guarantee, such as HomeBond's, that covers major structural defects in a new home for a set period.
A heating system divided into zones, each with its own thermostat or timer, so that rooms are heated only when needed.
The cost of acquiring the site and building the house, before the home is occupied.

factCards.term: Three factors that influence house design
factCards.definition: Aesthetic and environmental factors; present and future family requirements; initial and maintenance costs.

factCards.term: Four elements a BER assessor measures
factCards.definition: Room and window areas; wall thickness and insulation levels; the heating system; the floor and wall types.

factCards.term: Three points of the kitchen work triangle
factCards.definition: The sink, the cooker and the fridge.

factCards.term: Three areas covered by the Building Regulations
factCards.definition: Safety, materials and construction; insulation, heating and lighting; ventilation and waste.

factCards.term: Two protections given by HomeBond's scheme
factCards.definition: Cover for major structural defects in the home; protection of the buyer's deposit if a registered builder fails.

questions.prompt: State three features of house design that improve energy efficiency and explain how each reduces energy use.
questions.model: Insulation in the roof, walls or cavity reduces heat loss, so less fuel is needed to keep rooms warm. Double glazing reduces heat loss through windows. Zoned heating with thermostats and timers heats only the rooms in use at the times they are needed. Passive solar design, with south-facing glazing, captures solar heat for free. Any three features, each linked to a reduction in heat loss or energy use, earn the marks.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the suitability of a two-storey house with a ground-floor kitchen and living room, three upstairs bedrooms and one bathroom for a family of two adults and three young children, one of whom uses a wheelchair. Suggest two modifications.
questions.model: Suitability for the family: three bedrooms may be adequate for a family of five, but the children may share and need storage. Ground-floor kitchen and living room suit family life. The wheelchair user cannot reach the upstairs bedrooms or the single bathroom, so the layout is unsuitable without changes. Circulation and doors must be wide enough for a wheelchair. Aspect and energy efficiency: the house should be checked for south-facing living space and insulation. Modifications: provide a ground-floor bedroom and an accessible bathroom with level or ramped access and wide doors, or install a stairlift; lower switches and sockets; add a utility room or storage. Any two sensible modifications, justified for this family, earn the marks, and the evaluation should reach a conclusion on suitability.
